title: One Value Twice Another
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Return true if there are two different positions i and j with nums[i] === 2 * nums[j], and false otherwise.

The positions must differ, but the values may be equal. Negative numbers follow the same rule: −6 is twice −3.

examples.why: 6 at index 3 is twice 3 at index 1. The pair does not have to be adjacent or in any order.
0 is twice 0, but there is only one 0 and it cannot pair with itself.

hints: Checking every pair works but is O(n²). What would you like to look up in O(1)?
Walk the array keeping a set of values seen so far. For each x, which earlier values would make a matching pair?
Either an earlier value is 2x, or x is even and an earlier value is x / 2. Check both, then add x to the set.

explain.intuition:
For each value x there are only two partners that could pair with it: 2x (x is the half) and x / 2 (x is the double, only if x is even). A set of the values seen so far answers both lookups in O(1).

Checking against values seen earlier, before adding x, handles zero cleanly: a lone 0 never meets itself, while a second 0 finds the first one. Every pair is still found, because whichever of the two comes later sees the other in the set.
steps: For each x: if seen has 2 * x, return true.
If x is even and seen has x / 2, return true.
Add x to seen. After the loop return false.
pitfalls: Building the full set first and then checking each x for 2x. A single 0 then finds itself and returns true.
Checking x / 2 for odd x. In JavaScript 3 / 2 is 1.5 and never matches, but in Python 3 // 2 is 1 and wrongly matches a 1.
Checking only one direction (only 2x). In [2, 1] the double comes first.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over distinct positions.

solutions.title: Set of earlier values
solutions.idea: For each value, look up its double and (if even) its half among the values already seen.

solutions.title: Sort and binary search
solutions.idea: Sort, then for each position binary-search for twice its value at a different index. Uses no hash set.

followups: Find whether some value is k times another for a given k. What changes when k is 0 or 1?
Return how many index pairs (i, j) satisfy the rule, not just whether one exists.
